lead: A sensor must hand over what it measures as an electrical signal, and there are only two ways to do it. Either it makes its own emf (electromotive force, a generated voltage) from the measurand’s energy, or it changes its impedance and lets an external supply deliver the current. The first kind is active (self-generating), the second passive (externally energised), and this one label decides the wiring.
prereq: You need: basic circuits — Ohm's law, ideal voltage and current sources, and power P = VI = I²R.

blocks.text: A sensor responds to a physical quantity and gives an output that carries information about it. The quantity being measured is the measurand: the temperature of a bearing, the pressure in a pipeline, a patient’s pulse.

A transducer converts one form of energy into another. Every sensor is a transducer, but we say sensor when we care about the measurement and transducer when we care about the conversion. An actuator works the other way: electrical input, physical output, such as the solenoid that closes a valve. An inverse transducer converts an electrical input into a non-electrical output — for example a piezoelectric crystal driven by a voltage to launch ultrasound, or the pen motor that moves the pen of a chart recorder.
Most measurement devices follow the same chain, from the physical world to a number on a display:

items: Measurand — the quantity to be measured, for example the temperature of a bearing.
Sensing element — the part that first responds, such as a diaphragm or a thermistor bead.
Variable-conversion element — turns that response into an electrical variable: resistance, charge, inductance or emf.
Variable-manipulation element — amplifies, filters and converts it, ending as a voltage or a digital count.
Output stage — a display, a recorder or a controller input.

blocks.text: Some syllabi call this the general input-output configuration of a measurement system, or the functional elements of an instrument. A bedside blood-pressure channel shows all five: the measurand is arterial pressure; the diaphragm of the disposable transducer is the sensing element; a strain-gauge bridge on that diaphragm converts its bending into a voltage; an amplifier and filter manipulate it; the monitor shows 120/80 mmHg. Not every device has all five stages. A thermocouple produces an emf directly, so it needs no separate conversion element.

Classify by energy source and the answer is one of two words. An active sensor (also called self-generating) converts the measurand's energy directly into electrical energy. It needs no external supply. A passive sensor (also called externally energised) generates no signal of its own. It converts the measurand into a change of resistance, inductance or capacitance, and an external supply must be present for that change to become a signal.

items: Active: thermocouple (Seebeck emf), piezoelectric crystal (charge on stress), photovoltaic cell (light gives emf), tachogenerator (emf proportional to speed).
Passive: RTD (resistance temperature detector), thermistor, strain gauge, potentiometer, LVDT (linear variable differential transformer), photoconductive cell, capacitive sensor.

At the bedside: the piezoelectric crystal of an ultrasound probe receiving echoes is active; the thermistor of a temperature probe and the photodiode of a pulse oximeter, run with a bias supply, are passive.

blocks.text: The wiring consequence in one line: an active sensor is a voltage or charge source and needs a high-impedance load; a passive sensor is a variable impedance and needs excitation plus a bridge or divider.

blocks.where: ΔV is the signal in volts, I the excitation current in amperes and ΔR the change of sensor resistance in ohms; the current comes from the supply, not the sensor.

blocks.text: Two practical details follow. An active sensor’s output is often only millivolts, so the amplifier’s input impedance must be far larger than the sensor’s source resistance, or the emf is loaded down (worked example 2). For a passive sensor the excitation is a design choice: too small and the signal is buried in noise, too large and the current heats the sensor and shifts its own reading.

Energy source is the most useful split, but exams also ask for the others. By output form, a sensor is analog (a continuous voltage, like a thermocouple) or digital (pulses or a code word, like a shaft encoder); a digital signal resists noise on a long cable far better, though grounding still matters. By physical principle, sensors are resistive, inductive, capacitive, piezoelectric, thermoelectric, photoelectric or Hall-effect (see physical principles of sensing). By contact, a sensor touches the process (an RTD inside a tank) or does not (an infrared forehead thermometer); non-contact sensing suits moving, hot or sterile objects. By stage, a primary transducer turns the measurand into an intermediate non-electrical quantity and a secondary transducer turns that into an electrical signal: a Bourdon tube bends with pressure and moves the core of an LVDT, which gives the voltage. By application, we speak of industrial, biomedical, automotive or domestic sensors.

blocks.text: These axes are independent. The same RTD is passive, analog, contact and resistive at once, and a full description of a sensor uses every label that applies.

spec.aria: Two circuit panels. Left, active: a 25 millivolt source with a 500 ohm source resistance feeding an amplifier input; with 1 megohm the input is 24.99 millivolts, with 10 kilohms 23.81 millivolts. Right, passive: a 1 milliamp current source driving a Pt100 of 100 ohms, giving 100 millivolts and 0.10 milliwatts of self-heating.

examples.question: Classify each device as active or passive, and justify with one number where the data allows. (a) A Pt100 RTD reads 100.0 Ω at 0 °C and is run at 1 mA excitation. (b) A piezoelectric accelerometer gives 12 mV per g (g = 9.81 m/s², the acceleration due to gravity) with no supply connected. (c) A photodiode in photovoltaic mode gives 0.45 V in sunlight. (d) The same photodiode in photoconductive mode with 5 V reverse bias.
steps: (a) P = I²R = (1 × 10⁻³ A)² × 100.0 Ω = 1 × 10⁻⁴ W = 0.10 mW. That power comes from the external supply; the RTD only sets how much current flows. Passive, and the excitation fixes its self-heating.
(b) 12 mV per g appears with no supply connected, so the crystal turns the mechanical energy of the force into the signal. Active.
(c) 0.45 V in sunlight with no bias: light energy becomes electrical energy. Active.
(d) With 5 V reverse bias the supply drives the current and light only changes its size. Passive.
Rule: ask where the energy in the output comes from. Measurand: active. External supply: passive.
examples.answer: (a) Passive, self-heating 0.10 mW from 1 mA through 100.0 Ω; (b) active; (c) active; (d) passive.

examples.question: An active sensor has an open-circuit emf of 25 mV and a source resistance of 0.5 kΩ. What voltage reaches (a) an amplifier of input resistance 1 MΩ and (b) one of 10 kΩ? Give the loading loss of each in mV and %.
steps: The sensor and the amplifier form a divider between the source resistance R<sub>s</sub> = 500 Ω and the input resistance R<sub>in</sub>: V<sub>in</sub> = e × R<sub>in</sub>/(R<sub>in</sub> + R<sub>s</sub>).
Loss = 25 − 23.81 = 1.19 mV, which is 4.76 %: a calibration error far larger than most sensors’ accuracy class.
Rule: keep R<sub>in</sub> at least 1000 times R<sub>s</sub> to hold the loading loss near 0.1 % or less.
examples.answer: (a) 24.99 mV, loss 0.0125 mV (0.05 %); (b) 23.81 mV, loss 1.19 mV (4.76 %). An active sensor needs a high-impedance load.

traps: Marking a photodiode passive by habit. It is active in photovoltaic mode (no bias, light makes the emf) and passive in photoconductive mode (reverse bias, light changes the current).
Confusing the sensing element with the transducer. The diaphragm is the sensing element; the capacitive pressure transducer is the whole device with its terminals.
Calling a passive sensor “no power needed”. It makes no signal of its own and reads zero without excitation; it draws current from that supply, which is why the excitation level matters.
Writing 'active sensor' for any sensor that needs a power supply to run its amplifier. The label describes the sensing element only.

quiz.q: Define sensor, transducer and inverse transducer in one line each.
quiz.a: Sensor: responds to a measurand and gives an informative output. Transducer: converts one form of energy into another. Inverse transducer: converts an electrical input into a non-electrical output, such as a crystal launching ultrasound or the pen motor of a recorder.

quiz.q: Why does a passive sensor need excitation while an active one does not?
quiz.a: A passive sensor only changes its impedance; with no current there is no voltage to measure, so a supply must drive the current that the impedance modulates. An active sensor converts measurand energy into emf directly, so it is its own source.

quiz.q: Classify as active or passive: thermocouple, RTD, photovoltaic cell, LVDT, tachogenerator, strain gauge.
quiz.a: Active: thermocouple, photovoltaic cell, tachogenerator. Passive: RTD, LVDT, strain gauge.

quiz.q: A passive sensor of 250 Ω is excited at 2 mA. Its resistance changes by 0.4 Ω. Find the signal voltage.
The same photodiode is called active in one circuit and passive in another. Explain how both statements are correct.
quiz.a: Classification depends on the operating mode. With zero bias, light generates an emf across the junction, so the device is self-generating and active. With reverse bias, the supply provides the current and light only alters its magnitude, so the device is externally energised and passive.

quiz.q: A thermocouple and an RTD both measure a furnace at 600 °C. Which one is active, and what does that mean for the wiring and for the amplifier?
quiz.a: The thermocouple is active: it makes a small emf (tens of millivolts) with no excitation, so it goes to a high-impedance amplifier and needs cold-junction compensation. The RTD is passive: it needs an excitation current and a bridge or divider, and that current must stay low to limit self-heating.

beyond: Not for the exam. Self-powered sensors are a research area: a piezoelectric harvester under a footbridge or a thermoelectric patch on a machine powers a wireless node with no battery. MEMS (micro-electro-mechanical systems) chips put the sensing element and its circuit on one silicon die. Search next for energy-harvesting sensors.
